items.title: Ben Shapiro reassesses the president he campaigned for | Newsmakers
items.summary: Conservative host Ben Shapiro says he is holding to his conservative values in the unstable era of President Trump. The host of The Ben Shapiro Show voted against Trump in 2016 but also campaigned for him in 2024. He’s disappointed in the president’s tariffs, alleged corruption and the execution of the Iran war. “I regret the way the president has performed,” Shapiro tells host Steve Inskeep in this episode of Newsmakers . “I don't regret my vote. I don't have a time machine.” Shapiro says Trump’s aggressive immigration enforcement and the general “whiff of corruption” that surrounds the White House — specifically the Trump family’s crypto company World Liberty Financial — all contributed to the Republican Party’s midterm losses in Congress, governor's mansions and state legislatures. He believes that Republicans have an “uphill road in 2028” and that Vice President Vance isn’t the ideal Republican presidential candidate. He argues that Vance would shrink Trump’s winning 2024 voting bloc of Hispanics, the working class, women and college-educated individuals. Shapiro points to Secretary of State Marco Rubio as a potential 2028 Republican candidate with broader appeal and a larger coalition. But he says many within the current White House will likely be damaged by association. Shapiro also unpacks his new movie, Confession — featuring Rob Lowe and James Franco — and the recent decline in his show’s YouTube subscriptions.

items.title: South Korea education minister resigns over exam cheating scandal
items.summary: Choi Kyo-jin admits last-minute measures to stop AI-assisted cheating during the college entrance exam caused chaos.
items.body: South Korea's Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin has resigned over an exam cheating scandal that shocked the nation. He said he took full responsibility for the confusion caused by last-minute measures aimed at stopping AI-assisted cheating during Thursday's annual college entrance exam, known as Suneung.

items.title: Three killed and dozens missing after fire at Indonesian factory
items.summary: At least three people were killed and 36 are still missing after a fire at a confectionary factory.
items.body: At least three people have been killed and 36 are still missing after a fire at a confectionary factory in western Java on Saturday. Firefighters were still tackling some flames on Sunday, while rescuers searched for the missing in parts of the damaged building where workers were believed to be trapped.

items.title: An elevator, a brick wall and a bathroom: scientists use gravity to send ‘practically unblockable’ message
items.summary: Australian physicists chose to transmit the word ‘gravity’ in binary code through brick wall Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Australian scientists have used gravity as a means of communication, in a proof-of-concept experiment involving a snail-paced 1950s elevator, a brick wall and a men’s bathroom. Physicists at the University of Queensland have used gravity to transmit a “practically unblockable” message about 70cm through a brick wall, by sending an elevator up and down between two floors and measuring changes in the gravitational field as a result of the movement.

items.title: CEO of funding agency for UK science and research criticised by union over cuts
items.summary: Exclusive: Prospect’s Mike Clancy tells Ian Chapman at UKRI that union has ‘lost confidence’ in his leadership A trade union that counts scientists and engineers among its members says it has lost confidence in the leader of the UK’s national funding agency for science and research, citing concerns about plans for major cuts. The letter from Mike Clancy, the general secretary of Prospect, to Ian Chapman, the chief executive of UK Research and Innovation (UKRI), is the latest development in a row over changes in funding for projects and research facilities.
items.body: A trade union that counts scientists and engineers among its members says it has lost confidence in the leader of the UK’s national funding agency for science and research, citing concerns about plans for major cuts.

items.title: Senate committee rejects Trump nominee to lead National Science Foundation
items.summary: Committee chair Bill Cassidy, a Republican, said Jim O’Neill ‘did not do enough to stand up for science’ in previous posts Jim O’Neill will not undergo a confirmation hearing on Wednesday to head he National Science Foundation (NSF) because he “did not do enough to stand up for science” in his previous position, said Bill Cassidy, a Republican from Louisiana who is chair of the Senate committee on health, education, labor and pensions. This ends O’Neill’s run for the top US scientific organization, an embattled independent federal agency that has seen major budget cuts and grant freezes under the Trump administration . The next NSF nominee will face a Democratic-led Senate.
